title: What a free-flying foundry feels in each orbit: drag, lifetime, sunlight
question: How quiet (residual drag acceleration), how long-lived and how sunlit is each candidate low-Earth-orbit band for a free-flying foundry, measured from 68 years of tracking data?

headline.text: From 253 million tracking records: drag on a foundry-sized free-flyer (our assumed BC 150 kg/m2) at 500-525 km is about 16 nano-g in active-Sun years and 1.5 nano-g in quiet years, 60-670 times below the ISS 1 micro-g requirement.

datasets.license: CC BY 4.0 (GFZ; Matzka et al. 2021, Space Weather 19, e2020SW002641); F10.7 from NRCan / DRAO Penticton
datasets.notes: Daily observed F10.7; we use an 81-day centred mean (F10.7a) and the daily Ap.

datasets.name: NRLMSIS 2.1 empirical atmosphere (pymsis 0.13)
datasets.license: open source (pymsis, MIT-style; NRLMSIS distribution terms)
datasets.notes: Empirical model driven by the observed F10.7/Ap; used for the foundry rescaling and lifetimes after checking it on the measured decay (Starshine 3, population solar response).

method: Downloaded all 68 yearly parquet files of the Space-Track TLE mirror (12.5 GB) plus CelesTrak SATCAT and GFZ F10.7 to Engaging scratch (mit_data_transfer).

Per year (16-CPU job): semi-major axis a = (mu/n^2)^(1/3) from each element set's mean motion; kept debris, rocket bodies and payloads flagged non-operational, e < 0.01, mean altitude 150-1000 km, skipping the first 30 days after launch.
For each element set, paired it with the first set of the same object at least 4 days later (3-8 day gap), da/dt = delta a / delta t; dropped pairs with |delta a| > 30 km (cross-tags).
Took the median da/dt per object and calendar month (>= 3 pairs, altitude spread < 40 km); a_d = -(da/dt) v / (2a), v = sqrt(mu/a), g-level = a_d / 9.80665.
Cross-checked against the TLE mean-motion-derivative field (n-dot/2): median ratio of the two decay-rate estimates 0.95, IQR 0.84-1.03 over 1.4 million object-months (stats.ndot_cross_check).

Grouped object-months by 25 km band and by solar-activity tercile of the 81-day F10.7; statistic = median over months of within-month medians, 95% CI by bootstrapping months (months, not objects, are the independent units, since all objects in a month share one atmosphere).
Foundry scaling: a_d = 0.5 rho v^2 / BC for BC = m/(Cd A) = 50, 150 (central), 400 kg/m2, with rho the orbit-averaged NRLMSIS 2.1 density at each band's centre and the tercile-median F10.7 and Ap.

Checked that model route on data: (i) against the measured decay of the Starshine 3 sphere (known 91 kg, 0.94 m; BC ~ 60 kg/m2), pair by pair with that day's F10.7 and Ap; (ii) the measured high/low-tercile drag ratio of the passive population vs the model's ratio, band by band.
Tried and rejected a B*-based density route (B* tracks the solar cycle ~30x, so it is not a ballistic coefficient); details in stats.rejected_route_bstar.
Lifetime: integrated da/dt = -a rho v / BC day by day with NRLMSIS 2.1 driven by the observed daily 81-day F10.7 of 1990-2026 (wrapped), from start dates every month 1990-2014, down to 180 km.
Kaplan-Meier: residence time of real debris and rocket bodies from first crossing below each altitude (after 1990) to the SATCAT decay date, censored at 2026-10-01.
Power: analytic beta angle and cylindrical-shadow eclipse fraction for each candidate orbit through 2027 with J2 node regression, checked by brute-force propagation.

charts.caption: Our computation on public data. Each point is the median over calendar months of the within-month median a_d = -(da/dt) v / 2a for debris and rocket bodies on near-circular orbits (e < 0.01) in that 25 km band. Solar terciles use the 81-day F10.7: low < 83 sfu, high >= 131 sfu. Thin lines show the 10th (low activity) and 90th (high activity) percentile object-months: debris fragments with large area-to-mass ratios feel far more drag than compact bodies. The foundry curves are 0.5 rho v^2 / BC with NRLMSIS 2.1 density (model, checked against the measured decay of the Starshine 3 sphere and the population's solar response) for m/(Cd A) = 150 kg/m2 (our assumption; scale by 150/BC for other designs). Drag is only one part of the quasi-steady budget: gravity gradient adds about 0.39 micro-g per metre of radial offset from the centre of mass at these altitudes, and the ISS requirement lines are for the ISS, not a demonstrated free-flyer environment.

charts.caption: Simulation driven by real solar data, checked on measured decays. The foundry curves integrate da/dt = -a rho v / BC with NRLMSIS 2.1 density and the observed daily 81-day F10.7 of 1990-2026 (wrapped after 2026); the spread is the start date in the solar cycle. The green and grey lines are measured: Kaplan-Meier medians of how long real rocket bodies and debris that crossed each altitude after 1990 took to reenter (censored at 1 Oct 2026). They carry those objects' own ballistic coefficients (rocket bodies behave like BC ~ 50, debris lower), not a foundry's.

charts.caption: Analytic geometry (simulation, not tracking data). Dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbits stay in sunlight except for a short eclipse season around the June solstice; 51.6 deg and 53 deg orbits enter Earth's shadow on most orbits. Non-SSO curves use a starting node of 0 deg; their annual statistics barely depend on it (stats.node_spread). Penumbra and atmospheric refraction are ignored.

solar_terciles_F107a_sfu.reference_period: 1990-01-01 to 2026-10-24, 81-day centred mean of observed F10.7

rejected_route_bstar.what: Effective density from rho = 2 a_d / (v^2 B), B = 12.741621 B* (Hoots & Roehrich 1980 nominal conversion), object lifetime-median B*.
rejected_route_bstar.why_rejected: Median B* of the same population at 500-550 km swings ~30x with the solar cycle (e.g. 6.6e-5 in 2009 vs 2.8e-3 in 2002), i.e. B* absorbs atmospheric-density error and is not a physical ballistic coefficient. The resulting density was 3-35x NRLMSIS (ratio growing with altitude) and gave lifetimes far shorter than real rocket bodies show, so it is not used.

foundry_ballistic_coefficient_assumption.rationale: Central: a ~10 t free-flyer with ~30 m2 mean projected area including arrays (10000/(2.2*30) ~ 150 kg/m2). Low: lighter body with large face-on arrays. High: compact dense module with arrays edge-on. Drag acceleration scales exactly as 1/BC, so any other design is a linear rescale.

gravity_gradient_micro_g_per_m.note: radial gravity-gradient term 3 n^2 r per metre offset from the centre of mass (our analytic computation)

iss_reference_published.quasi_steady_requirement: 1 micro-g magnitude and 0.2 micro-g perpendicular component, below 0.01 Hz, in at least 50% of payload rack locations, for 180 days/yr in 30-day increments; transient limits 1000 micro-g peak and 10 micro-g-s per 10 s per axis (Del Basso et al., AIAA 2003-1002, NASA NTRS 20100042410; ISS SSP 41000).
iss_reference_published.assembly_complete_verification: 14 of 32 payload rack locations met the quasi-steady requirement in analysis; the 15th and 16th were at 1.11 and 1.17 micro-g (same source).
iss_reference_published.measured_environment: Quasi-steady accelerations below 0.01 Hz are 'on the order of less than a micro-g'; the unisolated vibratory spectrum reaches 'well over 10 milli-g' at the high-frequency end, isolation reduces it by up to 100x; structural modes are quieter during crew sleep (McPherson, Hrovat, Kelly, Keller, NASA ISS Researcher's Guide: Acceleration Environment, NP-2015-11-040-JSC).

iss_acceleration_data_probe.result: not openly downloadable from our environment on 2026-10-24
iss_acceleration_data_probe.detail: PIMS documents its PAD archive at http://pims.grc.nasa.gov/ftp/pad (SAMS, MAMS, MMA). The pims.grc.nasa.gov host did not resolve from MIT Engaging or from a home network; the gipoc.grc.nasa.gov/pims/ftp/pad mirror returned HTTP 403 for the root and dated paths; the 'pub/pad' link resolves to a documents page. No crew-sleep vs awake contrast was computed; we cite the PIMS published characterisation instead.

findings: In the 500-525 km band, drag on a foundry-like free-flyer (ballistic coefficient 150 kg/m2, our assumption) is about 1.6e-08 g in the high solar-activity tercile and 1.5e-09 g in the low tercile (6e-09-5e-08 g at solar high for BC 400-50). That is 62 to 667 times below the ISS 1 micro-g quasi-steady requirement (published).

Altitude and the Sun matter about equally: the same foundry would feel 7.4e-08 g (solar high) and 1.1e-08 g (solar low) at 400-425 km, and 4.0e-09 and 3.0e-10 g at 600-625 km. Measured decay of passive objects rises 12x from the low to the high solar tercile at 500-525 km.

Measured directly from 15,573 passive objects (debris and rocket bodies, with their own ballistic coefficients), the median object in the 500-525 km band decelerates at 1.0e-07 g in high solar activity (95% CI 9.0e-08-1.2e-07, bootstrap over 145 months) and 8.9e-09 g in low activity; those objects behave like a ballistic coefficient of about 24 kg/m2, so a heavier foundry feels proportionally less.

The model route used for the foundry curves is checked against our data two ways: NRLMSIS 2.1 reproduces the measured decay of the Starshine 3 sphere (known mass and size, BC 60 kg/m2) with a median measured/model ratio of 0.87 (IQR 0.81-0.92, 48 ten-day windows, 2001-2003); and its solar-activity response is close to the measured one (measured/model ratio of high-to-low drag 0.60-1.22 across the 300-625 km bands).

Drag is not the binding microgravity constraint for a free-flyer above about 400 km: gravity gradient alone is about 0.4 micro-g per metre of radial distance from the centre of mass (3 n^2 r, our analytic computation), so cartridge placement near the centre of mass and the absence of crew, exercise and pumps (vibratory regime, which on the ISS reaches over 10 milli-g at high frequency without isolation, published) matter more than the altitude.

A dead foundry (BC 150) reenters on its own in about 2.14 years from 400 km, 5.62 from 450 km, 12.3 from 500 km (range 6.95-18.6 with solar phase), 25.9 from 550 km and 50.6 from 600 km. Only below about 443 km does a BC-150 foundry meet the 5-year post-mission disposal rule (FCC 2022, published) without propulsion; a light BC-50 design meets it up to about 506 km and a dense BC-400 design only below 392 km. Real rocket bodies took a median 3.7 years to reenter after crossing 500 km and 0.5 after 400 km (Kaplan-Meier, measured), close to the model's BC-50 values (4.49 and 0.695 yr).

Power and heat: a dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit is sunlit 94% (500 km) to 96% (600 km) of the year with 96-106 eclipse days and about 1,430-1,613 thermal cycles per year (eclipses at most 22.7 min, around the June solstice), versus 66% sunlight and ~5,514 cycles for an ISS-like 51.6 deg orbit and 69% and ~5,119 for a 53 deg Starlink-like orbit, with eclipses up to 36.0 min every orbit (analytic geometry, simulation).

Candidate band, as our computation and not a design decision: on these numbers a dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit at about 525-575 km balances the four constraints best if the foundry carries a deorbit capability. At 550 km, drag on a BC-150 foundry is 8e-10-9e-09 g, sunlight 95% with ~1,521 thermal cycles a year (vs ~5,514 at 51.6 deg), and 955 catalogued objects sit within 25 km (vs 9,924 in Starlink's 450-500 km region just below). Trade-offs: a dead BC-150 foundry would stay up ~26 years there (~10 for BC 50), far beyond the 5-year rule, so disposal must be propulsive. The alternative, an ISS-like ~420 km orbit, self-disposes in ~3 years and has only 546 neighbours, but drag is ~7x higher (still < 0.1 micro-g), it needs reboosts, and it sees 66% sunlight and ~5,514 eclipses a year. SSO launch costs more delta-v than 51.6 deg and has no crew-station access; and the result rests on public TLE crowding, an assumed BC and a model atmosphere checked on one sphere.
limitations: The measured objects are debris and rocket bodies, not foundries. Their g-levels are real measurements; the foundry curves rescale them through a model atmosphere (NRLMSIS 2.1) and an assumed ballistic coefficient, checked against one known-BC sphere (Starshine 3, solar-maximum years only) and the population's solar response. The absolute level is therefore uncertain by roughly the Starshine spread plus the BC assumption, which dominates (a factor 8 across BC 50-400).

TLE B* could not be used as a ballistic coefficient: it tracks the solar cycle (~30x), so per-object ballistic coefficients of the measured population are not known; we only infer an effective population value through the model.
Co-rotation of the atmosphere lowers the relative speed by ~4% (v^2 by ~8%) for 51.6-53 deg orbits and raises it slightly for sun-synchronous orbits; the foundry curves use the inertial speed.

TLE mean elements smooth over each fit span; the result is an orbit-averaged, quasi-steady (<< 0.01 Hz) along-track drag. It says nothing about vibration, attitude-control, venting or crew disturbances, and does not include the gravity-gradient and rotational terms that depend on where a cartridge sits relative to the centre of mass.

Some 'non-operational' payloads may have manoeuvred earlier in life; debris can be cross-tagged. Medians per object-month and the 30 km jump cut limit, but do not eliminate, these effects. Results for payloads are kept separate (stats are dominated by debris and rocket bodies).
Solar terciles pool three solar cycles (22-25). Cycle-to-cycle differences and geomagnetic storms (e.g. the 2024 May storm) are inside the spread, not modelled separately.
Lifetimes assume a constant BC, no attitude change and the 1990-2026 solar sequence repeated; real decays depend on future cycles. They are a planning estimate, not a disposal analysis.
Power/thermal uses circular orbits and a cylindrical shadow (no penumbra, no atmosphere), which slightly underestimates eclipse length (< 1 min).
ISS acceleration data (PIMS) could not be downloaded today; ISS numbers are published values, not our computation.
future_big_data: CelesTrak SupGP: operator-supplied ephemerides for Starlink, OneWeb, Kuiper and others, to measure shell occupancy and manoeuvre rates at higher fidelity than TLEs.

GRACE-FO and Swarm accelerometer Level-1B/ACC data (ESA/NASA/GFZ): direct measurement of non-gravitational acceleration at 400-500 km, to replace the B*-based density route with measured densities and to see orbit-period variations a free-flyer would feel.

Conjunction screening for a foundry fleet: propagate candidate foundry orbits against the full catalogue (or SupGP) for a year to count close approaches per shell, and estimate avoidance manoeuvres (which themselves disturb microgravity).
Space-Track decay and reentry messages (TIP) to calibrate the lifetime model on known-ballistic-coefficient spheres (ANDE, Starshine-class objects).
ISS PIMS SAMS/MAMS PAD archive, if access is restored: crew-sleep vs awake vibratory spectra as the baseline a crew-free foundry would beat.
NOAA SWPC solar-cycle-25/26 forecasts to replace the repeated 1990-2026 F10.7 record in lifetime estimates.
